nodes.name: Controlling idea
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

levels.1: Makes a general claim with an unclear focus.
levels.2: Establishes a clear claim that addresses the prompt, with an uneven focus.
levels.3: Establishes and maintains a clear, specific, and credible claim that addresses all aspects of the prompt.
levels.4: Establishes and maintains a precise, substantive claim that addresses all aspects of the prompt. Acknowledges limitations and/or the complexity of the issue or topic.

nodes.name: Selection and citation of evidence
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

levels.1: Includes minimal details from sources. Sources are used without citation.
levels.2: Includes details, examples, and/or quotations from sources that are relevant to the claim. Inconsistently cites sources.
levels.3: Includes details, examples, and/or quotations from sources that support the claim and supporting ideas. Consistently cites sources with minor formatting errors.
levels.4: Includes well-chosen details, examples, and/or quotations from sources that fully support the claim and supporting ideas. Consistently cites sources using appropriate format.

nodes.name: Development / explanation of sources
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

levels.1: Explanation of ideas and source material is irrelevant, incomplete, or inaccurate.
levels.2: Explains ideas and source material to support the argument, with some incomplete reasoning or explanations.
levels.3: Accurately explains ideas and source material and how they support the argument.
levels.4: Thoroughly and accurately explains ideas and source material, using logical reasoning to support and develop the argument.

nodes.name: Organization
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

levels.1: Lacks an evident structure. Makes unclear connections among claims, reasons, and/or evidence.
levels.2: Groups ideas and uses transitions to develop the argument, with some lapses in coherence or organization.
levels.3: Groups and sequences ideas to develop a cohesive argument. Uses transitions to clarify the relationships among claim(s), reasons, and evidence.
levels.4: Groups and sequences ideas in a logical progression in which ideas build to create a unified whole. Uses varied transitions to clarify the precise relationships among claim(s), reasons, and evidence.

nodes.name: RI.11-12.6: Determine point of view or purpose
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

levels.1: Partially or inaccurately determines author’s point of view or purpose.
levels.2: Accurately determines author’s point of view or purpose.
levels.3: Accurately determines author’s point of view or purpose with some connection to rhetorical context 2.
levels.4: Accurately determines author’s point of view or purpose and demonstrates how the point of view or purpose relates to a specific rhetorical context.

nodes.name: C3 concept: founding and legal documents
nodes.source: LDC Student Work Rubric — Argumentation Task, Grades 11–12 · exported from CoreTools 09/23/2024

1: Identifies parts of the U.S. Constitution, other founding documents, laws, or treaties that are relevant to a topic/issue.
When relevant, makes a reasonable connection between founding documents and other relevant laws, rules, or policies.
When relevant, identifies an idea or principle from founding documents, laws, or treaties that is relevant to a topic/issue.
2: Provides a general summary of the intended purpose of parts of the U.S. Constitution, other founding documents, laws, or treaties relevant to a topic/issue, and describes an impact on relevant nations or groups.
When relevant, describes the relationship of ideas/principles in founding documents to those found in other relevant laws, rules, or policies (past or present).
When relevant, applies an idea or principle in founding documents, laws, or treaties in generally appropriate ways to make sense of a topic/issue.
3: Accurately explains the purpose and content of parts of the U.S. Constitution, other founding documents, laws, or treaties relevant to a topic/issue, including the historical context that shaped their intended purpose, and explains their impact on relevant nations or groups.

When relevant, explains the significance of ideas/principles in the founding document to the development of other relevant laws, rules, or policies (past or present), and explains whether/how the ideas or principles have changed in different contexts.

When relevant, applies an idea or principle from founding documents, laws, or treaties in ways consistent with their intended legal or political role/function to support an explanation or make an evidence-based claim about a topic/issue.
4: Accurately explains with specific details the purpose and content of parts of the U.S. Constitution, other founding documents, laws, or treaties relevant to a topic/issue, including their precise meaning or purpose in historical context, and their impact on relevant nations or groups.

When relevant, draws precise and explicit connections between ideas/principles from a founding document and other laws, rules, or policies (past or present), and explains with precision whether/how the ideas or principles have changed in different contexts.

When relevant, applies and precisely interprets relevant founding documents, laws, or treaties in ways consistent with their intended legal or political role/function to support an explanation or make an evidence-based claim about a topic/issue.
